stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the clinic to discuss his father, who has recently been diagnosed with a glioma. He is concerned about mobile phone use. Which of the following is the optimal way to study the relationship between mobile phone use and glioma?
options: Cell culture in the presence of electromagnetic radiation
Comparison of incidence rates of glioma versus mobile phone use
Prospective case–control study
Retrospective database analysis
Rodent study to establish the relationship
explanation:
Prospective case–control study
A prospective case–control study is the optimal way to assess any link between mobile phone use and development of glioma. It is the preferred option because cases and controls can be matched closely for other risk factors apart from use of the mobile phone itself. Glioma is a rare tumour and any incremental risk is likely to be small from mobile phone use if it is present at all. Large studies are therefore likely to be needed.

Cell culture in the presence of electromagnetic radiation
Cell culture in the presence of electromagnetic radiation is likely to be highly misleading, with great difficulties in replicating the exact conditions of radiation exposure to the side of the head from a mobile phone. Dependent upon experimental conditions, any study may raise false concerns or falsely reassure about the effect of mobile phones on brain tumour risk.

stem: A randomised controlled trial has been conducted to evaluate fish-oil capsules against corn-oil capsules (as a control group) to determine the antihypertensive effects in a group of mild, untreated hypertensive patients. How are the results of this study best summarised?
options: Mean and confidence interval for the difference in reduction in blood pressure between the two
Means and confidence intervals for the reduction in blood pressure in each of the treatment groups
Means and standard deviations for the blood pressures before treatment and after treatment in each
Separate levels of significance for each treatment to evaluate whether the blood pressure has been
The significance level of a test to compare blood-pressure changes in the two treatment groups
explanation:
Mean and confidence interval for the difference in reduction in blood pressure between the two
treatments As the study is controlled, it is the difference between the active intervention group and the control that is of importance. A randomised controlled study is where subjects are allocated at random (by chance alone) to receive one of several clinical interventions. One of these interventions is the standard of comparison or control. The control may be a standard practice, a placebo ("sugar pill"), or no intervention at all. In this case, this option would provide the most statistical information to best summarise the results.

Separate levels of significance for each treatment to evaluate whether the blood pressure has been
significantly reduced in each case Separate levels of significance for each treatment to evaluate whether the blood pressure has been significantly reduced in each case is incorrect. This option describes bad practice, as separate tests for the two treatment arms are inappropriate

stem: A patient is admitted with a suspected DVT. The patient has a high clinical score giving a pretest probability for DVT of 2/5 (40%). If a clinical test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80% to detect DVT, what is the post-test probability for this patient if the test is negative?
explanation:
1/13
The negative likelihood would be: Negative LR = (100 – sensitivity) / specificity, (100 – 90)/80 = 10/80 = 0.125 The formula for calculation of post-test probability: (post-test odds/[Post-test odds + 1]) Whereas post-test odds = (pre-test odds × LR) and pre-test odds = (pre-test probability/ [1 – pre-test probability]) By putting the values in it we get: pre-test odds = (40/[1 – 0.4]), = 0.66 post-test odds = 0.66 × 0.125 = 0. post-test probability = 0./ 0. + 1 = 0./ 1. = 0.077= 1/13

stem: In a randomised controlled trial comparing selenium supplementation with placebo in patients with a history of basal-cell or squamous-cell carcinomata of the skin, the primary outcome measure is the incidence of basal-cell or squamous-cell carcinomata at 1 year. Which one of the following tests is most appropriate to assess this outcome?
options: Analysis of variance
Chi-squared test
Mann–Whitney U-test
McNemar test
Student’s t-test
explanation:
Chi-squared test
A chi-squared test is used to compare binary outcomes (in this case, incidence or no incidence of carcinoma) in independent groups (BCC and SCC).

Analysis of variance
Analysis of variance is incorrect. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) uses continuous outcome measures and compares the means of multiple groups,

McNemar test
McNemar test is incorrect. The McNemar test compares binary outcomes for two paired (dependent) groups, but this study is comparing independent groups.

stem: A letter published in a journal suggests an established antidepressant may cause photosensitivity. This is based on a personal case series. The manufacturer wishes to determine as quickly as possible whether this is a true association. Which one of following techniques is most appropriate?
options: A case-control study
A dose-ranging study
A double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled study
A meta-analysis
A prospective cohort study
explanation:
A meta-analysis
A meta-analysis involves looking and analysing existing published trials. In particular, it would look at safety data and adverse events of rash or photosensitivity from placebo and active arms of the clinical studies. A meta-analysis would facilitate a quick and also most effective study to establish whether there was a true association between the use of an anti-depressant and photosensitivity.

A double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled study
A double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled study is incorrect. For this to take place you would need to randomly allocate subjects to one of two groups, anti-depressants (experimental) and placebo (control). For it to be double-blind, both the investigator and the patient cannot know which group they are in. These trials are very good studies but are time-consuming and the question asks for a study that will determine whether there is a true association rapidly.

stem: In an RCT, 1000 patients were randomised to receive either an active drug or a placebo. Of the 500 randomised to placebo, 30 dropped out during the study. Of the 500 randomised to the active drug, 20 dropped out during the study. The results are to be analysed on an ‘intention to treat’ basis. What is the final sample size in each arm in the analysis?
options: 490 treatment, 480 placebo
490 treatment, 500 placebo
500 treatment, 500 placebo
510 treatment, 480 placebo
510 treatment, 490 placebo
explanation:
500 treatment, 500 placebo
In an ‘intention to treat’ analysis, all patients allocated to either the treatment or the placebo arm of the study are analysed, even if they dropped out of the study prematurely. As such, although 470 in one arm, and 480 in the other arm actually finished the study, it is 500 in each arm who are analysed. The analysis is performed to reduce the bias seen when only completers are analysed as in this case the response to therapy is exaggerated.

490 treatment, 480 placebo
490 treatment, 480 placebo is incorrect. You have probably given this answer because you have taken 10 patients away from the number that have dropped out, then subtracted this number from the number of patients initially recruited into each arm.

stem: In a study of the effect of cannabinoids in reducing pain in multiple sclerosis, participants were asked to rate their level of pain on a scale of 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable). Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: The pain scale is a continuous measurement
The pain scale is a nominal measurement
The pain scale is an interval measurement
The pain scale is an ordinal measurement
The pain scale is a dichotomous measurement
explanation:
The pain scale is an ordinal measurement
An ordinal measurement consists of a number of categories that have a natural order but the actual values are meaningless. If a patient gives a score of 2, then their pain is worse than if they had given a score of 1. However, the difference between a score of 1 and 2 may not be the same as between a score of 2 and 3 (the order is meaningful but not the value).

The pain scale is a continuous measurement
The pain scale is a continuous measurement is incorrect. A continuous measurement has meaningful values (e.g. age) and does not have discrete groups.

The pain scale is an interval measurement
The pain scale is an interval measurement is incorrect. An interval measurement is the result of dividing a continuous measurement into groups (e.g. age groups).

stem: Which one of the following best describes a 95% confidence interval?
options: The interval that contains the p-value with 95% confidence
The measure of significance of study results
The period between treatments in a crossover trial
The range within which 95% of the sample value lies
The range within which we are 95% confident the population parameter lies
explanation:
The range within which we are 95% confident the population parameter lies
A 95% confidence interval (CI), by definition, means we would expect the true population parameter to fall within the interval estimates 95% of the time.

The interval that contains the p-value with 95% confidence
The interval that contains the p-value with 95% confidence is incorrect. The p-value is a value that is not expected to be found within this CI apart from by chance. The p-value can be used to denote statistical significance (usually when p<0.05) but is not essential when dealing with CIs, which can exhibit statistical significance on their own.

The range within which 95% of the sample value lies
The range within which 95% of the sample value lies is incorrect. The 95% CI means we are 95% certain the true mean value lies within the range stated.

stem: After treatment with one of two antihypertension agents in a randomised controlled trial testing the effectivness of a new antihypertensive against an existing treatment (50 patients per treatment group), the changes in diastolic blood pressure appear to be approximately symmetrically distributed within each treatment group. Which one of the following statements is most appropriate for analysis of the trial data?
options: A paired sample t-test should be applied to test the null hypothesis that both treatments produce
An independent sample t-test should be applied to test the null hypothesis that the same mean
As the results may not be normally distributed, a non-parametric test for independent samples, such
As the results may not be normally distributed, a non-parametric test for paired samples, such as the
The changes in blood pressure should be assessed as being of clinical significance or not, and a Chi-
explanation:
An independent sample t-test should be applied to test the null hypothesis that the same mean
reduction in diastolic blood pressure occurs with each treatment An independent sample t-test compared the mean of two independent groups (i.e. two anti-hypertensive treatments). It analyses whether there is statistical evidence that associated population means are significantly different. Data should be normally distributed for the t-test to be applied.

As the results may not be normally distributed, a non-parametric test for independent samples, such
as the Mann–Whitney U-test, should be applied

stem: To establish up-to-date ‘normal range’ values, untreated forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV 1) was measured in 1000 individuals selected at random from the general population. The FEV 1 was found to follow a normal/Gaussian distribution, with a mean of 3.50 litres and a standard deviation (SD) of 0.75 litres (standard error of 0.02). What range of FEV 1 covers 95% of individuals?
options: 1.25–5.75 litres
2.00–5.00 litres
2.75–4.25 litres
3.46–3.54 litres
3.48–3.52 litres
explanation:
2.00–5.00 litres
2.00–5.00 litres is correct. This is the mean ± 2 SDs. The SD is a measure of the spread of values in a particular population that is being studied. In a normal distribution: around 68% of values lie within ± 1 SD of the mean around 95% of values lie within ± 2 SDs of the mean (exactly 50% are within ± 1.96 SD) and 99.72% of values lie within ± 3 SDs of the mean.

3.46–3.54 litres
3.46–3.54 litres is incorrect. This is the mean ± 2 standard errors. The standard error measures how accurately a sample distribution represents a population.

stem: You are working on an attachment in drug surveillance and concern has been raised because the yellow-card scheme has revealed two cases of hepatic failure associated with a new treatment for rheumatoid arthritis that has been launched some 11 months earlier. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to establish any causal relationship?
options: Further phase 3 studies
Meta-analysis of existing data
National disease registry
Post-marketing surveillance study
Yellow-card reporting
explanation:
Meta-analysis of existing data
The answer is meta-analysis, which pools existing data in order to establish a larger patient database from which to draw conclusions regarding the occurrence of adverse effects.

Further phase 3 studies
Further phase 3 studies is incorrect. Although further phase 3 studies may deliver data on abnormal liver function, the number of patients needed to allow sufficient power to detect a causal relationship, and the duration of follow up, is likely to be prohibitive.

National disease registry
National disease registry is incorrect. A national disease registry will deliver data on disease time course and complications with respect to multiple different interventions, but it is likely to be difficult tofor control confounders in individual patients when making conclusions about the data.

stem: In a randomised, controlled, parallel group trial to compare two treatments for lowering blood pressure, comparison of the mean ages at the time of randomisation shows an average difference of 3 years between the two treatments. A t-test shows that the difference is highly significant (P < 0.01). Which one of the following statements is most likely to be true?
options: An analysis should be undertaken to see if the imbalance alters the conclusions of the trial
Extra patients should be recruited and randomised to the treatments in such a way that a balance in
The patients should have been stratified by age when undertaking the randomisation
The validity of the trial is compromised
This should be ignored as we know the allocation to treatment was at randomisation
explanation:
An analysis should be undertaken to see if the imbalance alters the conclusions of the trial
No matter how well-designed a trial and how well-thought out the randomisation, sometimes imbalance in a baseline variable between study groups will still occur. In the case of this question, there is a significant difference in average age, so this difference cannot be ignored. Therefore, the approach suggested in in this option is a reasonable one to take, as if the imbalance does alter the conclusions of the trial, its results could be invalidated due to bias.

Extra patients should be recruited and randomised to the treatments in such a way that a balance in
Extra patients should be recruited and randomised to the treatments in such a wayChat that a balance with in mean age is achieved

The validity of the trial is compromised
The validity of the trial is compromised is incorrect. We do not know if the trial is invalid based on the information that we have been given and without any extra analysis of results.

stem: You are asked to undertake a review of heart failure prescribing in comparison to clinical guidelines within the Hospital Trust. You are examining evidence for the use of aldosterone antagonists in the treatment of heart failure. The Randomised Aldactone Evaluation Study (RALES) trial demonstrated that adding the aldosterone antagonist spironolactone to an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor reduced all-cause mortality by 30% (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.60% to 0.82%; p< 0.001; ARR 11%). According to these figures, what is the number needed to treat (NNT) for the use of spironolactone in the treatment of heart failure with respect to all-cause mortality?
explanation:
10
The number needed to treat in the RALES trial is calculated by dividing 100 by the absolute risk reduction, which in this case calculates to 9.09 (100 ÷ 11); however NNT is always rounded up to the next whole number, which is 10.

18
The number needed to treat in this study is 9, given that the absolute risk reduction was 11% and the NNT is calculated as 100 ÷ absolute risk reduction, which is 9.

stem: A series of trial results are presented for a novel lipid modifying agent used in addition to maximal tolerated statin therapy with respect to any reduction in Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE). Which of the following studies has demonstrated the greatest reduction in absolute risk?
options: 33% relative risk reduction versus a placebo event rate of 1%
15% relative risk reduction versus a placebo event rate of 3.5%
10% relative risk reduction versus a placebo event rate of 2%
20% relative risk reduction versus a placebo event rate of 2.5%
10% relative risk reduction versus a placebo event rate of 3%
explanation:
15% relative risk reduction versus a placebo event rate of 3.5%
For this you need to work out the absolute risk reduction for all 5 options: 33% RRR versus PER of 1% - ARR = 0.33 x 1 = 0.33% 15% RRR versus PER of 3.5% - ARR = 0.15 x 3.5 = 0.525% 10% RRR versus PER of 2% - ARR = 0.1 x 2 = 0.2% 20% RRR versus PER of 2.5% - ARR = 0.2 x 2.5 = 0.5% 10% RRR versus PER of 3% - ARR = 0.1 x 3 = 0.3% 15% relative risk reduction versus a placebo event rate of 3.5% has the highest ARR of 0.525%.

10% relative risk reduction versus a placebo event rate of 2%
10% relative risk reduction versus a placebo event rate of 2% is incorrect. This option only gives an ARR of 0.2%.

stem: In 200 consecutive patients attending a Diabetic Outpatients Clinic, 27 are found to have diabetic retinopathy. Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: The incidence of diabetic retinopathy in diabetics in the UK is 13.5%
The incidence of diabetic retinopathy in this population was 13.5%
The prevalence of diabetic retinopathy in diabetics in the UK is 13.5%
The prevalence of diabetic retinopathy in this population was 13.5%
This study does not provide any information on the incidence or prevalence of diabetic retinopathy
explanation:
The prevalence of diabetic retinopathy in this population was 13.5%
The incidence is the number of instances of a given illness commencing or of persons falling ill during a given period in a specified population. The prevalence is the total number of instances of the illness during a given period in a specified population. An easy way to calculate 27/200 as a percentage is to divide 27 by 2 = 13.5%. This question only tells us that these patients have diabetic retinopathy, and not they these are new cases, so we are concerned with the prevalence, rather than the incidence. We can only give this statistic for this particular population and we cannot generalise it to the entire UK population.

This study does not provide any information on the incidence or prevalence of diabetic retinopathy
This study does not provide any information on the incidence or prevalence of diabetic retinopathy is incorrect. The question does provide us with information regarding prevalence of diabetic retinopathy in this particular population.

stem: Investigators hypothesise that lower staffing levels in intensive therapy units (ITUs) at night may lead to worse outcomes for patients admitted at night than those admitted during the day. An observational cohort study of all ITU admissions is planned to investigate this hypothesis. Which would be the best method to control for selection bias in analysing the results of this study?
options: Blinding
Case-mix (risk) adjustment
Double-data entry
Randomisation
Repeated measurement
explanation:
Case-mix (risk) adjustment
Selection bias occurs when the chance of being assigned a particular treatment depends on factors that are linked to the outcome. For example, if patients who are at higher risk of dying are more likely to receive a new treatment then a study comparing the risk of death in patients receiving the new treatment to those who are not will be biased against the new treatment. The best way to remove selection bias is through randomisation. However, this is not possible in some cases. We cannot randomise the time when patients are admitted to ITU, but we can control the analysis for known confounding factors – this is called ‘case-mix (or risk) adjustment’. For example, patients admitted to ITU following elective surgery are known to be at very low risk; they are also more likely to be admitted during the day than the night. We should therefore include surgical status as an explanatory variable in the model.

Double-data entry
Double-data entry is incorrect. Double-data entry will improve the accuracy of the data but will not affect selection bias.

stem: Concern has been expressed that people who live near overhead electricity power cables are at increased risk of developing a cancer. What would be the best design for a study to investigate this concern quickly?
options: A cross-over RCT
A group comparative randomised controlled trial (RCT)
A prospective cohort study
A retrospective case-control study
An observational survey
explanation:
A retrospective case-control study
This study compares people with the cancer (cases) against those that don’t (control). It involves retrospectively comparing the two groups looking at frequency of exposure to the risk factor (electricity power cables) and developing cancer. This is a particularly good study design to use in this case as it is a quick, feasible way of carrying out the study without putting participants at risk. It is good for studying rare conditions as well as looking at multiple risk factors (i.e. age, time living in the area). However, the study is reliant on a subject’s memory and can lead to recall bias, as those with cancer will be more likely to recall any possible risk factors.

A prospective cohort study
A prospective cohort study is incorrect. This design has many advantages. You would be able to match people from both groups (either living close to or far away from overhead electricity cables) taking into account any confounding factors. These people would be followed up for a long time (10-20 years) and this is where the problem lies. In this case when dealing with a risk factor causing cancer, you would want a more urgent result and this makes this study design less desirable.

stem: Which one of the following statements best describes a type-2 error?
options: Alpha error
Risk of a false-positive result
Risk of detecting a treatment difference when there is none
Risk of not detecting a significant difference when there is one
None of the above
explanation:
Risk of not detecting a significant difference when there is one
A type-2 (also known as beta error) occurs when the null hypothesis is incorrectly accepted, i.e. a false- negative.

Alpha error
Alpha error is incorrect. An alpha (or type-1 error) is the incorrect rejection of a true null hypotheses, i.e. a false- positive.

Risk of a false-positive result
Risk of a false-positive result is incorrect. This is describing a type-1 error rather than a type-2 error.

Risk of detecting a treatment difference when there is none
Risk of detecting a treatment difference when there is none is incorrect. This is actually describing an alpha (type-1) error.

stem: In an audit of renal biopsies, there were 17 complications in 54 biopsies performed by consultants (31%) and 6 complications in 49 biopsies performed by registrars (12%). The complication rates are compared using a Chi- squared test, reported as ‘Chi 2 = 5.5, p = 0.02’. How should these results be interpreted given the skill sets of the two groups?
options: In a given biopsy in the future, a complication is significantly more likely to occur if it is performed by
In a given biopsy in the future, a complication is significantly more likely to occur if it is performed by
We cannot draw any conclusion on complication rates in future biopsies as consultants may have
We cannot draw any conclusion on complication rates in future biopsies as no information has been
We cannot draw any conclusion on complication rates in future biopsies as the numbers are too
explanation:
We cannot draw any conclusion on complication rates in future biopsies as consultants may have
performed more difficult biopsies in the audit Although the complication rate for consultants in the audit was significantly higher than for registrars (p = 0.02), this may have been because the consultants were performing more technically difficult procedures. This is an example of selection bias, which can be a major problem in statistical analysis of audit data. To remove such a bias completely it is necessary to randomise patients to either consultant or registrar, but this is moving more towards a trial design, rather than a clinical audit. Some attempt to remove the bias could be made by adjusting for factors that are known to be associated with a higher risk of complications.

stem: In a study the prevalence of a disease in people who smoke is 25/100. This means which one of the following?
options: A larger sample is needed
For every 4 who smoke, 1 has the disease
For every 5 who smoke, 1 has the disease
Smoking causes disease
The disease occurs 4 times more often in those who smoke
explanation:
For every 4 who smoke, 1 has the disease
The incidence is the number of instances of a given illness commencing or of persons falling ill during a given period in a specified population. The prevalence is the total number of instances of the illness during a given period in a specified population. 25/100 as a fraction can be simplified to ¼. In this particular population of smokers, this means that 1 in 4 study subjects suffer from the disease of interest.

A larger sample is needed
A larger sample is needed is incorrect. We are looking at prevalence and not comparing differences between groups, so sample size is not an issue here.

Smoking causes disease
Smoking causes disease is incorrect. We cannot infer causation from a raw statistic of prevalence.

stem: A 73-year-old man is admitted to the hospital after suffering a left carotid territory stroke. His blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg and he is in sinus rhythm with a pulse of 65 bpm. On carotid duplex it appears there is a stenosis which is amenable to surgical therapy. He asks you about the risks of surgery versus intensive medical therapy. On reviewing the trials you note that in one analysis the two year incidence of stroke in the surgical intervention group was 8%, versus 18% in those who had medical intervention only. How would you calculate the number needed to treat over 2 years with surgery to prevent 1 stroke?
explanation:
100/(18−8)
The number needed to treat (NNT) is the number of people that need to receive a treatment for one person to benefit. The NNT= 1/absolute-risk reduction. Absolute-risk reduction = medical (control) group incidents (18) – surgical intervention group incidents (8) = 0.18 – 0.08 = 0.10 NNT = 1 / (0.1) = 10

8/18
8/18 is incorrect. This is actually describing the relative risk (% of events in the surgical group/% of events in medical group) rather than the NNT.

stem: Treatment X is licensed as an effective treatment for lung cancer. The pharmaceutical company that markets treatment X believes it has a beneficial effect on quality of life. Before embarking on a full-scale randomised controlled trial, the company tested its hypothesis in an open study restricted just to patients prescribed treatment X. Each patient completed a validated quality-of-life scale at the start of treatment and then 12 months later. The scale gives integer values between 0 and 50; scores above 30 are considered to be desirable. Which one of the following methods is best for presenting the results from this study?
options: Average change in scale scores, with its 95% confidence limits
Change in the proportion of patients with scores above the desired cut-off level, with its 95%
Chi-square test and p-value for pre- and post-study proportions above the desired cut-off level
Mean scores at the start and end of the treatment period, with their standard deviations
Unpaired t-test statistic and p-value only
explanation:
Average change in scale scores, with its 95% confidence limits
Confidence intervals can be computed for either the mean or median change, depending on the distribution of the scores. If the confidence interval does not contain the value zero (the result that would occur if the treatment does not affect quality-of-life scores), the change can be accepted as statistically significant. More importantly, the confidence interval indicates the most likely range of values for the true population effect of treatment X on quality of life. Therefore, confidence intervals are more informative than a significance test in this instance, so this option is the correct answer.

Change in the proportion of patients with scores above the desired cut-off level, with its 95%
confidence limits Change in the proportion of patients with scores above the desired cut-off level, with its 95% confidence limits is incorrect. Reducing results to binary (or dichotomous) outcomes as in this option reduce statistical accuracy.

stem: A study is investigating the relationship between body mass index and systolic blood pressure in a group of individuals. Which one of the following graphical methods would best illustrate the results?
options: Bar chart
Box and whisker plot
Histogram
Pie chart
Scatter plot
explanation:
Scatter plot
In a scatter plot, two continuous variables are plotted against one another. A scatter plot of systolic blood pressure against body mass index (BMI) would show any relationship between the two.

Bar chart
Bar chart is incorrect. A bar chart would be a good choice to demonstrate the mean systolic blood pressure in discrete BMI categories (e.g. underweight, normal, overweight, obese), but is not a good choice to present two continuous variables.

Pie chart
Pie chart is incorrect. A pie chart is used to illustrate percentages and proportions, so would not be appropriate for this question.

stem: A study seeks to find an association between increasing perceptions of pain (ranked on a scale of 1–10) and increasing heart rate. Which one of the following measures is most appropriate?
options: Analysis of variance
Chi-squared test
Pearson’s correlation coefficient
Student’s T test
Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient
explanation:
Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient
Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient measures the correlation between the ranks of two variables. As it only compares ranks and not values, it is appropriate for use on an ordered categorical (ordinal) variable such as the perception of pain.

Analysis of variance
Analysis of variance is incorrect. Analysis of variance tests for a difference in mean values between a number of groups. It would tell us if the mean heart rate is different for different pain rankings, but not whether increasing pain is associated with increasing heart rate.

Pearson’s correlation coefficient
Pearson’s correlation coefficient is incorrect. Pearson’s correlation coefficient (often called ‘R’) is a measure of association between two continuous scale measurements. The measure of pain is not on a continuous scale, so this is not the best measure.

stem: In a cohort study of 1000 non-smokers and 1000 smokers, 450 of the smokers and 50 of the non-smokers developed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). What is the relative risk of smoking for COPD?
explanation:
9
The question asks the candidate to calculate the relative risk. Relative risk compares the disease risk (i.e. COPD) in people exposed to a certain factor (i.e. smokers) with disease risk in those who have not been exposed to the factor in question (i.e. non-smokers). The relative risk is calculated by the following formula: Relative risk (RR) = (incidence among exposed)/(incidence among unexposed) Therefore: Incidence among exposed = 450/1000 = 0.45 and Incidence among unexposed = 50/1000 = 0.05. The relative risk = 0.45/0.05 = 9.

7
7 is incorrect. Relative risk compares the disease risk (i.e. COPD) in people exposed to a certain factor (i.e. smokers) with disease risk in those who have not been exposed to the factor in question (i.e. non-smokers). To calculate the relative risk, the incidence among exposed is divided by the incidence among unexposed.

options: A randomised double-blind trial of increased inhaled steroid versus the addition of long-acting beta-
An open-label study of increased inhaled steroid therapy
A consensus statement from a group of experts
A retrospective chart analysis
An observational study
explanation:
A randomised double-blind trial of increased inhaled steroid versus the addition of long-acting beta-
agonist therapy Evidence-based medicine is concerned with using scientific evidence in order to inform clinical decisions. An important part of this is the hierarchy of evidence available to us, known as the levels of evidence. Levels of evidence for a therapeutic study (taken from National Center for Biotechnology Information ( Level Type of evidence 1A Systematic review (with homogeneity) of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) 1B Individual RCT (with narrow confidence intervals) 1C All of none study 2A Systematic review (with homogeneity) of cohort studies

stem: A research group evaluate the performance of two regional hospitals by analysing the mortality rates of patients admitted with pneumonia in the winter months. Two hospitals are selected for a direct comparative study Hospital A, a University hospital and Hospital B, a general hospital, with the research group focussing on patients from hospital admission to in-hospital death. The research group concludes that Hospital A has a greater mortality rate for pneumonia than Hospital B, therefore Hospital B must be superior. Which of the below answers explains the bias that this study may be exposed to most?
options: Selection bias
Lead time bias
Measurement bias
Recall bias
Socio-economic bias
explanation:
Selection bias
While the study concludes that Hospital A has a greater mortality, more information must be sought to determine admission criteria regarding pneumonia. For example, Hospital B may have a smaller ITU and less access to specialist care, with hospital A only taking the sickest patients. Therefore, a degree of scepticism must be applied to the conclusion that 'Hospital B must be superior'. More information must be sought to avoid admission rate bias.

Measurement bias
This refers to how information is gathered and affects the information collected. Knowing the measurement can affect performance particularly with observational studies.

stem: A new lipid modifying agent is in a clinical trial, you have recruited 3200 patients into the study assuming that it will reduce cardiovascular events by approximately 17.5%. You are warned by the data monitoring committee that the effect size may be less than 17.5%. What is the risk when you reach the end of the study?
options: The study is overpowered
Type-1 error
Type-2 error
You will need to re-open recruitment
You will need to stop the study because of lack of effect
explanation:
Type-2 error

stem: A new smoking-cessation therapy is found to increase quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) compared with standard therapy by an average of 1.2 QALYs at a cost of £35,000 per QALY gained. Which one of the following conclusions can be drawn from this information?
options: An additional 1.2 lives per year could be saved if the government invested £35,000 in funding this
Patients receiving the new therapy lived an average of 1.2 years longer than those who did not
The new therapy improved smokers’ quality of life
The new therapy is cost-effective
To decide whether the new therapy is cost-effective requires a value judgement
explanation:
To decide whether the new therapy is cost-effective requires a value judgement
Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) take account of both the quality of life and the length of life. A QALY is an adjustment of life expectancy that reduces the overall life expectancy by amounts that reflect the existence of chronic conditions causing impairment, disability and/or handicap as assessed from health survey data, hospital discharge data etc. The smokers who received the new therapy may either have lived longer or had an improved quality of life or some combination of these, but we are unable to determine which from the information presented. The total cost of funding this intervention also cannot be determined, as we would need to know how many patients would be eligible to receive the new therapy and at what cost. We do know that every £35,000 will improve outcomes by one QALY. Whether this is an appropriate use of money requires a value judgement, as there is only a finite amount of money available and it may be better spent on other interventions. Only if it is decided that £35,000 per QALY is an acceptable cost could we conclude that the therapy is cost-effective. It has been suggested that NICE use a threshold of £30,000 per QALY to determine cost-effectiveness; however, the new therapy would not be considered cost-effective with this cut-off.

stem: A cross-over trial is being planned to compare the efficacy of two drugs in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. Which one of the following design considerations should you adopt?
options: A washout period, where the patient receives placebo, should take place between the administration
If either drug is thought to be a disease-modifier, plans to run a cross-over trial should be abandoned
Only patients who will guarantee to complete both treatments should be recruited
The design should be simplified by avoiding randomisation as patients receive both treatments
There should be a run-in period when the patient receives a placebo
explanation:
If either drug is thought to be a disease-modifier, plans to run a cross-over trial should be abandoned
A Cross-over study is an interventional study in which all study participants receive the same treatment but at different times. This is done by switching the treatment and control groups therefore no study participants are left untreated. If any treatment in a cross-over trial is a disease-modifier (in the most extreme case, kills or cures the patient), then the interpretation of results in any subsequent period becomes impossible. This is because disease modification implies that one course of the drug will permanently change the future timecourse of that patient's disease in some way, making a cross-over study un-interpretable. In this case a parallel trial is the only appropriate option.

The design should be simplified by avoiding randomisation as patients receive both treatments
The design should be simplified by avoiding randomisation as patients receive both treatments is incorrect. This would simply be bad practice, as only by randomisation of the treatment order can we be assured that we are guarding adequately against bias.

Proportional hazards models are a type of survival analysis concerning the amount of time that occurs before an event occurs to one or more covariates that may be associated with that quantity of time. stem: D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product that can be detected in the blood after thromboembolism. The D dimer test can be useful to rule out a diagnosis of pulmonary embolism; if the test is normal, the patient is unlikely to have a pulmonary embolism. What quality of the D-dimer test does this describe?
options: Negative predictive value
Positive predictive value
Precision
Reliability
Specificity
explanation:
Negative predictive value
The negative predictive value is calculated by the ratio of the number of true negative results to the total number of negative results (true plus false). Therefore, a test with a high negative predictive value can accurately predict that a person with a negative result will not have the disease. In the context of D-dimer tests, a negative D-dimer makes it very unlikely that a patient has a pulmonary embolism.

Precision
Precision is incorrect. Precision is in fact another term for positive predictive value. The precision of a test is calculated by the ratio of the number of true positive results to the total number of positive results (true plus false). Therefore, a test with high precision can accurately predict that a person with a positive result will have the disease. This is not the case for the D-dimer test, which has a high sensitivity but a low specificity; i.e. if there is a pulmonary embolism, the D-dimer is very likely to be positive. However, there are many reasons why a D-dimer can be positive besides a pulmonary embolism; hence it is not very specific. This leads to a high rate of false positives, and therefore it has a low precision in the detection of pulmonary embolism.

explanation:

It is good clinical practice to have an independent Data Monitoring Committee to review trial data as it progresses. A Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) is a group of people that reviews accumulating data in a clinical trial and advises the sponsor (directly or indirectly) on the future management of the trial. It mainly reviews safety and efficacy data but may also see quality and compliance data. The use of an independent DMC should be the default position. However, for some trials, e.g. a low-risk, short-term, randomised phase II trial, it might be appropriate for a non-independent committee or group within the same trials unit or company to review the data, provided that they are not members of the trial team (NHS guidance for research ethics committees).

Unpaired t-test
explanation:
Log-rank test
The log-rank test is used to examine the null hypothesis that the survival curves in the two groups are the same. That is to say that the test can demonstrate the likelihood that survival in the two groups across the study period is similar; if very unlikely (eg a low probability or P-value), then the null hypothesis can be rejected and a statistical difference in survival claimed between the two groups.

Analysis of variance (ANOVA)
Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is incorrect. ANOVA tests examine whether the means differ between multiple sets of data; it is similar to a t-test, but can consider more than two groups. This is a less powerful test than the log-rank test.

stem: You are reviewing the results of a new screening test for a metabolic abnormality, which is recognised to lead to accelerated cirrhosis in patients who drink up to 10 units of alcohol per week. The specificity of the screening test is 93% and the sensitivity is 92%. The prevalence of the abnormality is 1.2%. Which of the following is the positive predictive value (PPV)?
explanation:
14%
PPV is the (sensitivity x prevalence) / (sensitivity x prevalence + (1-specificity) x (1-prevalence)). For the present example, this is (0.92x0.012)/(0.93x0.012+0.07x0.988) = 14%. An alternative formula for calculating PPV is to draw an imagined two-by-two table of abnormality positive and negative (columns) and test outcomes (rows) to answer this: prevalence=1.2%, or 12 cases in 1000. Applying the given sensitivity and specificity to the column totals, the columns can be filled in. The PPV is then TP/(TP+FP), or 11/80=14%. stem: In a group of 80 subjects, measurements of diastolic blood pressure (DBP) are found to be approximately normally distributed with a mean of 74 mmHg and a standard deviation of 6 mmHg. Which one of the following statements is most likely to be true?
options: Approximately 13 subjects will have a measured DBP level that is less than 68 mmHg and 2 will
Approximately 27 subjects will have measured DBP levels above 80 mmHg
Approximately 40 subjects will have DBP levels between 68 mmHg and 80 mmHg
Nobody will have a DBP level of 90 mmHg or higher
There will be exactly 40 subjects with measured DBP levels higher than 74 mmHg and 40 patients
explanation:
Approximately 13 subjects will have a measured DBP level that is less than 68 mmHg and 2 will
have a BP that is above 86 mmHg The standard deviation (SD) is a measure of the spread of values in a particular population that is being studied. The smaller the standard deviation, the more closely-grouped the values. Remember: the mean is the arithmetic average of a population i.e. the sum of all values of a variable in a population, divided by the number of subjects in that population. In a normal distribution: Around 68% of values lie within ± 1 SD of the mean. Around 95% of the values lie within ± 2 SD of the mean. Exactly 95% of the values lie within ± 1.96 SD of the mean (i.e. 2.5% lie in each tail of the bell curve). Let’s work through this question now.

stem: Blood pressure is normally distributed. For a sample of 100 Asian women the average blood pressure is 50, standard deviation = 5, standard error = 1/2. Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: 10% of Asian women have blood pressure below 40 mmHg
We are approximately 95% confident that the population mean blood pressure for Asian women lies
Blood pressure measurement in Asian women is not informative
The mean blood pressure of Asian women must lie within the range (49, 51)
Approximately 95% of Asian women have blood pressures in the range (45,55)
explanation:
We are approximately 95% confident that the population mean blood pressure for Asian women lies
in the interval (49, 51) In a normal distribution: Around 68% of values lie within ± 1 SD of the mean. Around 95% of the values lie within ± 2 SD of the mean. Exactly 95% of the values lie within ± 1.96 SD of the mean (ie 2.5% lie in each tail of the bell curve). The 95% confidence intervals for the mean can be calculated by mean ±2SE (standard error). In this question, 95% of the population will fall within 2x5 ± 50 i.e. 40-60 mmHg. The 95% confidence intervals for the mean will be 2x0.5 ± 50 i.e. 49-51. Therefore, this option is the correct answer.

stem: Which one of the following statements concerning the distribution curve is accurate?
options: In any given distributions there is only one mode
The mean is a good measure of central tendency in skewed distributions
The mean is higher than the median in positively skewed distributions
The mode is the sum of all the scores divided by the number of scores
When there is an even number of numbers, the mode is the mean of the two middle numbers
explanation:
The mean is higher than the median in positively skewed distributions
In a normal distribution, mean = median = mode. In a skewed distribution: The mean is “pulled towards” the values in the outlying tail of the distribution and is unrepresentative of the bulk of the data. Skew is named according to the direction in which the tail points. If the distribution is skewed, the median is preferable as a summary of the data. Negative skew: mode>median>mean. Positive skew: mean>median>mode. The mean is greater than the mode in a positively-skewed distribution.

The mode is the sum of all the scores divided by the number of scores
The mode is the sum of all the scores divided by the number of scores is incorrect. This is describing the mean, Tutor not the mode.

stem: You are plotting baseline data on the population of patients recruited into a clinical trial for a new weight loss agent. The plan for the publication is to include data on characteristics such as weight, height and blood pressure. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to plot these characteristics?
options: Box and whisker plot
Histogram
Line graph
Pie chart
Scatter plot
explanation:
Box and whisker plot
A box and whisker plot depicts a range of values including sample minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and sample maximum. The box extends from the border of the lower quartile to the border of the upper quartile, with the median depicted as a horizontal line across it. Often in a weight loss trial there are significant outliers, and a box and whisker plot allows assessment of possible hypo and hyper responders.

Histogram
ChatItwith Histogram is incorrect. A histogram simply evaluates frequency of a variable in a given dataset. only gives one value and does not represent the range of data.

Line graph
Line graph is incorrect. A line graph has a series of data values (known as markers) that are joined together by straight lines. It is often used to demonstrate a trend over a period of time, i.e. weight over a 6 month period.

stem: You are approached by a drug company to advise on study design to investigate use of a novel anti-thrombotic in acute coronary syndrome. The agent is thought to be associated with reduced need for interventional procedures, although it may be associated with increased risk of haemorrhage versus conventional therapy. Which of the following analyses for the primary endpoint is likely to be most appropriate in evaluating the effect of therapy?
options: Completer analysis
Sensitivity analysis
Intention to treat analysis
Per-protocol analysis
Screened population
explanation:
Intention to treat analysis
In this situation, it is crucially important to account for patients who may have dropped out of the study due to adverse events associated with the novel therapy. These patients may have deviated from the protocol, suffered an adverse event (AE) which was reported, or just withdrawn their consent. For this reason the only way to ensure a robust evaluation of the novel therapy versus comparator is to include all patients for the analysis who were randomised (the intention to treat analysis). This form of analysis is very representative of what actually happens in the clinical setting.

Completer analysis
Completer analysis is incorrect. This form of analysis involves deleting any subjects with any form of incomplete data from the analysis. In this scenario, patient that were asked to stop the anti-thrombotic agent due to haemorrhage would be discounted as they did not complete the study. Deleting these patients from the study would introduce a significant bias and invalid inferences.

stem: A study is being planned to investigate the efficacy of antibiotics to reduce urinary catheter-associated sepsis in elderly male patients who are at risk of pressure sores. What study design is most appropriate?
options: Randomised double-blind, placebo-control trial
Open-label, RCT (randomised control trial) comparing antibiotics with no antibiotics
Prospective audit of antibiotic use and patient outcomes
Retrospective audit of patient notes
Unblinded, pragmatic RCT comparing the use of antibiotics in all patients with the usual practice
explanation:
Randomised double-blind, placebo-control trial
An audit, whether prospective or retrospective, would be confounded by the likelihood that antibiotics will be given to patients who are considered to be at higher risk of sepsis. Randomisation is necessary to remove this association. A pragmatic design would evaluate the effectiveness of introducing a protocol for giving antibiotics to this patient group. However, it would not evaluate the efficacy of antibiotics as some patients in the control arm may be given antibiotics as ‘usual practice’. To evaluate efficacy, antibiotics must be compared with no antibiotics. The least biased method is to use a placebo for the control arm in a double-blind trial.

Retrospective audit of patient notes
Retrospective audit of patient notes is incorrect. An audit (whether prospective or retrospective) would be confounded by the likelihood that antibiotics will be given to patients who are considered to be at higher risk of sepsis.

stem: A 48-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes visits you in the clinic and has brought with him a printout from the Internet about the Proactive study. He is demanding that he be commenced on pioglitazone 45 mg as it has a benefit with respect to cardiovascular disease. Relative-risk reduction for the combined end-point of death from any cause, non-fatal myocardial infarction (excluding silent) or stroke was 16%, absolute-risk reduction of 2.1% over 3 years. Which one of the following fits best with the numbers needed to treat (NNT) to avoid the combined end- point shown above?
explanation:
48
The NNT= 1/absolute-risk reduction= 1/0.021 = 47.6=48

2.1
NNT = 2.1 is incorrect. You may have got to this number by just quoting the absolute risk reduction. However, you needed to work out the NNT and this is always given as a whole number as it is not possible to split a person into a decimal point! The inverse of the absolute risk reduction will give you the NNT of 48.

stem: In a study of the recurrence of colorectal adenomas, 50 patients were randomised to receive daily aspirin and 50 to receive placebo. After 1 year, at least one adenoma was observed in 15 of the 50 patients who were receiving aspirin and 20 of the patients who were receiving placebo. What was the relative risk reduction associated with aspirin?
explanation:
25%
The relative risk is a common measure of association derived from epidemiological studies of causation, such as cohort and case-control studies. The relative risk expresses how many more times a disease of interest occurs in the group exposed to a particular risk factor compared to the group that is not. In a cohort study, the relative risk is calculated from the ratio of incidence rates in the exposed group and the non-exposed group: Relative risk = Incidence of the disease in the exposed group ÷ Incidence of the disease in the non-exposed group As such, because the relative risk is a ratio, the value is always positive. If there is no association, relative risk = 1 (unity). The absolute risk reduction is the difference in risk between the control and intervention groups. The relative risk reduction is the absolute risk reduction as a percentage of the risk in the control group. Working through this question:

stem: You are investigating the performance of a new rapid screening test for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. It is designed to give a result within 90 min that can later be confirmed by a laboratory blood test. The performance of 1 500 tests is shown below: Test result Coronavirus (COVID) No COVID Positive 525 100 Negative 25 850 What is the sensitivity of this test?
explanation:
95%
95% is the sensitivity – the ability of the test to correctly identify all the patients who have coronavirus. It is calculated by dividing the true positives by the true positives plus the false negatives and should be as high as possible; as this is a first-stage test, 95% would be considered acceptable.

stem: A team of consultants has identified a set of 10 clinical symptoms they believe may help an insurance company predict how long a person will be off work after suffering whiplash injury in a car accident. Each symptom is assessed separately as 0 = absent, 1 = present. To determine exactly how useful these 10 symptoms are, 200 patients with whiplash injuries were assessed within 7 days of their accident and then followed up until all had returned to work. Which one of the following methods is best for analysing the results from this study?
options: Logistic regression
Paired t-test comparing time off work with total symptom score
Pearson correlation coefficient of total symptom score against time off work
Series of one-way analyses of variance, with time off work as the outcome (dependent) variable and
Spearman correlation coefficient of total symptom score against time off work
explanation:
Logistic regression
Logistic analysis with time off work as the outcome (dependent) variable and all 10 symptoms as predictor (independent) variables, will determine which of the symptoms significantly – and, importantly, independently – predict time off work. The regression coefficients will also provide estimates of the relative weight of each symptom in the prediction. For example, if the regression coefficient for symptom X is double that of the coefficient for symptom Y, the weights allocated to symptoms X and Y when calculating total scores should reflect this. Ordinary linear regression may be acceptable since all patients were followed up until they returned to work. However, it may be more sensible to use Cox regression as this is designed specifically for the analysis of time to an event occurring. This would also allow the study to be terminated early if some patients had not returned to work when the study had to end (i.e. had a very severe injury), as it can correctly handle ‘censored’ data.

stem: Which one of the following most accurately reflects information from post-marketing surveillance of 10,000 patients given a new drug?
options: Adverse events profile
Cost–benefit analysis
Cost-effectiveness
Comparative therapeutic efficacy
Drug potency
explanation:
Adverse events profile
In the UK, the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and the Commission on Human Medicines (CHM) jointly operate the Yellow Card Scheme which highlights suspected problems or incidents such as adverse drug reactions. This scheme is important as often drugs are approved following small trials. A patient cohort of 3000 will only highlight reactions that occur in more than 1 in 1000. The post-marketing surveillance occurs in phase 4 of the clinical trial.

Cost–benefit analysis
Cost–benefit analysis is incorrect. This is an important area to review especially for a manufacturer when trying to promote a product or for a commissioning group when trying to assess whether they should offer a particular drug and is now being analysed alongside a clinical trial. However, post-marketing surveillance involves monitoring the safety of medicines under their usual conditions of use. It is carried out to identify any new safety concerns (hypothesis generating), and to confirm or refute these concerns (hypothesis testing).

stem: A study to look at the exposure factors for achalasia is being designed. It has been decided to undertake a case- control study. Which one of the following biases may affect the participants of the chosen study design?
options: Confirmation bias
Observation bias
Publishing bias
Recall bias
Selection bias
explanation:
Recall bias
Case-control study design compares subjects with the disease against those that do not (control). It involves retrospectively comparing the two groups, looking at possible risk factors for the disease. This is a particularly good study design to use in this case, as it is a quick, feasible way of carrying out the study without putting participants at risk. It is good for studying rare conditions, as well as for looking at multiple risk factors (eg age, time living in the area). However, the study is reliant on a subject’s memory and can lead to recall bias, as those with the disease are more likely to recall any possible risk factors, compared to those without the disease.

Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is where researchers look for information or patterns in data to confirm an idea that they already have. Although this is possible, recall bias is due to the participants’ interaction with the study, rather than the investigators.

stem: The average weight of a group of 100 patients is 60 kg, standard deviation 5 kg. Weights are normally distributed. The standard error of the weights is which one of the following?
options: 0.6 kg
5 kg
12 kg
Larger than the standard deviation
Smaller than the standard deviation
explanation:
Smaller than the standard deviation
In a normal distribution, the standard error (SE) = standard deviation (SD) / square root of n. In this question, n=100 so its square root is 10. SE = 5 / 10 = 0.5. Therefore, only this answer is mathematically correct.

Larger than the standard deviation
Larger than the standard deviation is incorrect. The formula for the standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square-root of n, so mathematically, the standard error cannot be greater than the standard deviation.

stem: In a trial of a new drug compared with standard therapy, the risk of complications in the control arm is 2.4% and the risk of complications in the treatment arm is 1.8%. What is the absolute risk reduction associated with the new treatment?
explanation:
0.6%
The absolute risk reduction is the difference in risk between the control and intervention groups. Therefore, this question actually consists of simple mathematics. Absolute risk reduction = 2.4 – 1.8 = 0.6%

1.8%
1.8% is incorrect. It simply restates the risk in the treatment arm, i.e. 1.8%.

33%
33% is incorrect. You have probably reached this answer by calculating 2.4/1.8, which gives 4/3, then subtracting 1 from this answer.

stem: A study in patients aged 75 and over measures the effectiveness of warfarin versus aspirin with regards to reduction of embolic stroke. After the study has closed the group treated with warfarin has a 1.2% risk of embolic stroke over the period of the trial, whereas those on aspirin have a 2.4% risk. What is the absolute risk reduction for warfarin versus aspirin in this study?
explanation:
1.2%
The absolute risk reduction (ARR) = standard treatment events (aspirin) – new treatment events (warfarin) = 2.4 – 1.2% = 1.2%.

2.4%
2.4% is incorrect. You may have erroneously obtained this figure by simply quoting the risk of having a stroke within the aspirin group. However this is not describing the absolute risk reduction.

50%
50% is incorrect. This is actually describing the relative risk. RR = new treatment events (warfarin) / standard treatment events (aspirin) = 1.2% / 2.4% = 50%.

stem: Which one of the following observations is very sensitive to extreme scores in a distribution?
options: 50th centile
Mean
Median
Mode
All are equally affected
explanation:
Mean
The mean is the sum of all values divided by the total number of values. Therefore if there are extreme scores this will affect the sum of values and therefore the overall mean.

50th centile
50th centile is incorrect. The centile refers to the ranking of a value. For example, if you placed 100 students in order of their exam marks the student at the 50 th centile would be the 50 th student in that line up. They would not be affected by students with an extremely low or high score.

Median
Median is incorrect. This is the same scenario as the 50 th centile. If the students are ranked according to the exam score, the pupil in the middle’s score is not affected by those students with extreme scores.

stem: You are investigating a new blood marker for predictive value with respect to diabetic nephropathy. The results of the screening test versus biopsy confirmed nephropathy are listed below: Biopsy positive Biopsy negative Screen test positive 305 25 Screen test negative 45 150 Which of the following is the correct calculation for the positive predictive value?
explanation:
92%
PPV= Number of people with DN & a positive test ÷ Total number of people with positive test. PPV = 305 ÷ (305 + 25) = 0.924…. ≈ 92%.

9%
9% is incorrect. This is actually describing the percentage of the sample with a false-negative test = 45/525 ≈ 9%.

stem: You are involved in developing a study protocol to test a new drug for heart failure, and wish to conduct a 6- month-long clinical trial. During this time you are hoping to detect adverse events that might be expected to occur with an incidence of 1 in 2000 patients or more frequently. How many patients would need to be recruited for treatment with the new drug to have a 95% chance of detecting the occurrence of one adverse event?
explanation:
6000
Roughly speaking, for a study to have 95% power to detect a certain adverse event in a clinical trial you would need to enrol around three times as many patients as the expected event frequency, so in this case 6000 patients would be needed. If the frequency expected was 1 in 10 000, then you would need to recruit around 30 000 patients and so on. The practicalities and costs of conducting very large-scale trials mean that most new drugs are registered after trials in only a few thousand patients at most; therefore, adverse events occurring with a frequency of 1 in 10 000 or less are often only detected after the launch of a drug. For this reason, new drugs are afforded ‘Black triangle’ status in the UK to signify the need for intensive monitoring and reporting of all adverse effects to the regulatory authorities via the ‘Yellow-card’ system.

12 000
12 000 is incorrect. This would reliably allow detection of adverse effects that occur in 1 in 4000 patients or more frequently.

stem: A linear regression analysis of data collected from a random sample of 200 normal healthy individuals found that, on average, a 20 kg greater weight was associated with a 5 mmHg (95% confidence interval 2 to 8 mmHg) increase in systolic blood pressure (SBP). How should this finding be best interpreted?
options: A person who weighs 60 kg will have a SBP that is 10 mmHg lower than a person who weighs 100
Losing weight will lower systolic blood pressure
Only a small increase in SBP was associated with a large increase in weight, so a much bigger study
The relationship between weight and SBP is linear
There is a statistically significant relationship between weight and SBP
explanation:
There is a statistically significant relationship between weight and SBP
Although there is no significant P-value given in the body of this question, the 95% confidence interval is very narrow. As its range does not include the value 0, we can conclude that the association in the question is significant.

A person who weighs 60 kg will have a SBP that is 10 mmHg lower than a person who weighs 100
kg

Losing weight will lower systolic blood pressure
Losing weight will lower systolic blood pressure is incorrect. Association does not imply causation. A patient could well lose weight and still find that their systolic blood pressure has not been reduced.

stem: A new screening test is to be applied in a population. The test has a sensitivity of 99% and a specificity of 90%. If the prevalence of the disease is 10 per 1000 population, on average what proportion of those that test positive will truly have the disease?
explanation:
1/11
Positive predictive value is the proportion of those in a specified population who test positive and actually have the disease. Negative predictive value is the proportion of those who test negative and do not have the disease. Example of contingency table containing data for a screening test: Diseased Disease-free Positive (possible disease) a b Negative c d The sensitivity is the proportion of true positives correctly identified by the test: = a / (a+c) The specificity is the proportion of true negatives correctly identified by the test: = d / (b+d) Therefore, as the positive predictive value is the proportion of those testing positive who actually have the disease: = a / (a+b) Another way of looking at this is: PPV = True positives / (True positives + false positives)

stem: A clinical trial was designed to compare the use of a heater probe plus injection of thrombin versus the use of a heater probe plus placebo injection into the bleeding sites of haemorrhagic gastric ulcers. Results showed 16 out of 127 patients required emergency surgery in the thrombin arm, and 13 out of 120 patients required emergency surgery in the placebo arm. An appropriate analysis would use which one of the following?
options: An unpaired t-test
Analysis of covariance
Chi-square test
Log-rank test
McNemar’s test
explanation:
Chi-square test
There is no easy way to think through this question – you need to know about basic types of statistical test and the types of study populations that you would apply them to. In the case of this question, results are given as proportion of outcomes in two different groups, so you can construct a 2x2 contingency table and use this to carry out a chi-square test to determine the differences in proportions between the two groups.

Analysis of covariance
Analysis of covariance is incorrect. Analysis of covariance (or ANCOVA) is a generalised linear model. It uses a mixture of linear regression and analysis of variance (ANOVA), which compares means between study groups. Again, this test would be inappropriate.

stem: A drug is developed for a chronic disease with no known cause. It is a new drug which has worked in mammal models, and appears to work in short-term studies. No toxicity seen yet, but there are concerns about bone marrow and liver toxicity. What sort of trial should be undertaken?
options: Case-control
Double-blind
None –withdraw drug as it may be unsafe
Open-labelled
Single-blind
explanation:
Double-blind
In this study design neither the subject nor the researcher know whether the subject is receiving the new compound or the placebo. This is the gold standard clinical trial design as it reduces reporting bias from both the subject and researcher.

Case-control
Case-control is incorrect. This is a retrospective, observational study design. It can be used to review factors that could explain drug mechanisms and side effects. However, in this case, the drug has only been used in short-term trials and may not provide the information required. Also, for this type of study, the researcher is dependent on the subject and can lead to recall bias, when the affected subject recalls more risk factors. This can be proportional to the degree that they are affected.

stem: A study was conducted to determine a consensus for management of patients with stable coronary artery disease. 38 research papers in peer-review English language journals were identified to investigate whether revascularisation improves prognosis compared with medical treatment among patients with stable coronary artery disease. Which of the following methods best describes the method of summarising this literature to best inform the management of stable coronary artery disease?
options: ANOVA (analysis of variance)
Chi-squared analysis
Meta-analysis
Pearson correlation
Regression analysis
explanation:
Meta-analysis
A meta-analysis is a statistical procedure for combining data from multiple studies, providing the clinical and statistical significance. Meta-analysis can be used to identify a common treatment effect in consistent studies to produce a more precise estimate of overall effect. It can also be used to identify the reason for variation when the effect varies between studies.

ANOVA (analysis of variance)
ANOVA (analysis of variance) is incorrect. ANOVA (analysis of variance) is based upon the variability ('variance') between the group means. It is an extension of the t test and compares means from three or more independent samples. Data is taken from a single study design providing one nominal variable and one or more interval variable.

stem: A group of patients attending an Outpatients Clinic have their systolic blood pressure measured before and after their appointment, and are asked to grade their satisfaction with the appointment. The variables recorded are: (i) sex, (ii) initial blood pressure, (iii) end blood pressure and (iv) satisfaction rating (graded A for satisfied, B for neutral and C for dissatisfied). What are the scales of measurement of each of these different variables?
options: (i) Nominal, (ii) continuous, (iii) continuous, (iv) ordinal
(i) Nominal, (ii) continuous, (iii) ordinal, (iv) nominal
(i) Nominal, (ii) ordinal, (iii) ordinal, (iv) ordinal
(i) Ordinal, (ii) continuous, (iii) continuous, (iv) nominal
(i) Ordinal, (ii) continuous, (iii) ordinal, (iv) continuous
explanation:
(i) Nominal, (ii) continuous, (iii) continuous, (iv) ordinal
A nominal variable consists of categories that have no natural order. A continuous (or scale) variable has meaningful numeric values that can be added and subtracted. And ordinal variable consists of ordered categories. In this question: Sex is a nominal variable Blood pressure (before and after) is a continuous variable Satisfaction rating is an ordinal variable.

stem: In a trial of a new antihistamine drug, 1 in every 5 patients treated (95% confidence interval for the number needed to treat (NNT) for reduced symptoms: 1 in 3 to 1 in 10) was found to have significantly reduced symptoms on a validated hayfever symptom score two weeks after commencing the drug, compared with placebo. What is the most correct interpretation of the results of this study?
options: 5% of patients did not have reduced symptoms after 2 weeks on the new drug
The effect of the new drug is not significantly different from placebo
The ‘number needed to treat’ (NNT) statistic presented is inappropriate for this type of study
The statistical significance of this result cannot be determined as no P-value is reported
We can be 95% certain that between 10% and 33% of patients will benefit from the new drug
explanation:
We can be 95% certain that between 10% and 33% of patients will benefit from the new drug
A 95% confidence interval (CI) means there is only a 5% chance of the true mean value lying outside our range. In this case we know that the 95% confidence interval is 0.1-0.33 (from NNT of 1 in 3.3 to 1 in 10) meaning we can be 95% sure that 10-33% of patients benefit from the new drug.

The ‘number needed to treat’ (NNT) statistic presented is inappropriate for this type of study
The ‘number needed to treat’ (NNT) statistic presented is inappropriate for this type of study is incorrect. NNT is a useful statistic to use in this case. It describes the number of people needed to treat to for one subject to benefit.

81%
Sensitivity = True positives / (true positives + false negatives) which equals 65/ (65+15) = 81%. The specificity is TN/(TN+FP) which is 15 / (15+5) = 75%. The positive predictive value (PPV) is also important in this type of test, to avoid significant patient anxiety when no underlying carcinoma is present. The PPV is calculated to be 65 / (65+5) = 93%. The negative predictive value for this test is 15/ (15+15), which equals 50%. This is clearly of significant concern because a number of cases may be missed if this test alone was used as the screen for breast cancer.
